evidence_quotes.quote: This article explores the French water management experience by looking specifically at the interrelation between the public and private sectors in the provision of water and sanitation in historical perspective.

However, this contribution aims to illustrate the crucial importance of multi-level governance for the achievement of good water services, which is arguably more important than the ongoing public versus private debate in water policy.

At the beginning of the twentieth century important changes took place, whereby it became the norm that long-term infrastructure works (in particular, pipelines) would be owned by local authorities, while private or semi-public operators would only be responsible for operation and maintenance (in this case with a management contract).

Sewerage remained a non-commercial service for a longer period mainly for hygiene reasons. Connection to a main sewer was compulsory for households, and therefore it was covered by local taxes (as in Germany).
However, there is no evidence to ascertain which model is better at handling the crucial problem of social solidarity.

criterion_notes.c1: Discusses the historical development and municipal/inter-communal provision of drinking water supply and sewerage services in France, including historical extension of piped household water and rural connections.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — examines institutional, administrative, legal, and governance arrangements in French water and sanitation provision (municipal responsibility, inter-communal joint boards, centralisation vs decentralisation, delegation contracts, Conseil d'Etat jurisprudence, and public accounting rules). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes/borderline — discusses utility ownership and delegation contract structures (concession, affermage, management contracts), compulsory household sewer connection, public accounting depreciation rules, and tariff/cost-recovery mechanisms (generalised metered billing vs tax-funded subsidies), though framed as a macro-historical institutional narrative of sector organisation rather than a direct analysis of rule-type barriers at the household access margin. Under both readings, the paper is excluded as E05 because it lacks empirical evidence.
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical methodology, primary data collection, or systematic empirical synthesis is present. The article is a narrative historical and policy essay drawing on secondary historical sources and citing a few aggregate national descriptive figures (IFEN-SCEES 2004).
criterion_notes.c4: Does not empirically measure or evaluate an outcome of household/community access, connection, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion; mentions only high-level historical/sector background statistics in passing and explicitly states that there is no evidence to ascertain which management model better addresses social solidarity.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, sample frame, and analytical exposure-outcome framework; written as a narrative historical/policy overview.

study_design: Narrative historical and policy overview (non-empirical essay)
population_and_sample: not reported (narrative historical overview of French communes, joint boards, and water/sewerage utilities)
exposure: Municipal centralisation/decentralisation, inter-communal joint boards, delegation to private companies (concession, affermage, and management contracts), public accounting depreciation rules, and tax-subsidised vs metered user-charge financing
outcome: not reported (narrative discussion of historical network expansion and institutional organisation of utilities without empirical access outcome measurement)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the article discusses French municipal water and sanitation provision, utility ownership/delegation contracts, inter-communal joint boards, and cost-recovery/billing history, it is a non-empirical historical and policy overview essay with no empirical data collection, no analytical study design, no systematic synthesis method, and no empirical evaluation of service access or affordability outcomes. It is therefore excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 wording.
